lead: A four-stroke engine gives the piston four separate jobs (intake, compression, power, exhaust) and needs two crankshaft revolutions for one cycle. A two-stroke engine does the gas exchange near the bottom of the stroke, through ports in the cylinder wall, and finishes a cycle in one revolution. The choice decides how often each cylinder fires, how much fuel escapes unburnt and how the engine is built. Both SI and CI engines are made in both forms, so this chapter covers four engines: four-stroke SI and CI, and two-stroke SI and CI.
prereq: You need TDC, BDC and the part names from engine terminology and components.

blocks.text: A stroke is one travel of the piston between TDC and BDC, which is half a crankshaft revolution, or 180° of crank angle (°CA). Four strokes take 4 × 180° = 720°CA, two revolutions.

items: Intake (suction): the piston moves TDC → BDC with the inlet valve open; the falling pressure draws in fuel-air mixture (SI) or air alone (CI).
Compression: both valves closed, BDC → TDC. Pressure and temperature rise. Near the end, the spark fires (SI) or fuel is injected (CI).
Power (expansion): the burning gas drives the piston TDC → BDC; this is the only stroke that gives work to the crank.
Exhaust: the exhaust valve open, BDC → TDC; the rising piston pushes the burnt gas out.

blocks.text: The four-stroke SI and CI engines differ only in what enters in the intake stroke and how burning starts. Each cylinder gives one power stroke per 720°CA, and the flywheel carries the crank through the three idle strokes. In a real engine the valves open before and close after the dead centres; see valve and port timing diagrams.

sections.h3: Two strokes, one revolution: the crankcase-scavenged SI engine

blocks.text: The small two-stroke petrol engine has no valves. Three ports in the cylinder wall are opened and closed by the moving piston: the inlet port into the sealed crankcase, the transfer port from the crankcase to the cylinder, and the exhaust port from the cylinder to the silencer. The crankcase is the pump. Figure 1.3.1 shows the piston near BDC.

items: Upward stroke (BDC → TDC): the piston first covers the transfer port and then the exhaust port, and compresses the charge above it. Below, the crankcase volume grows, its pressure falls below atmospheric, and fresh mixture flows in through the inlet port (or a reed valve). The spark fires just before TDC.

Downward stroke (TDC → BDC): the burning gas drives the piston down, the power stroke. Below, the piston compresses the mixture in the crankcase. Near the end the piston edge uncovers the exhaust port first, and most burnt gas rushes out (blowdown). Then it uncovers the transfer port, and the compressed mixture flows from the crankcase into the cylinder and pushes out the rest of the burnt gas. This sweeping is scavenging.

blocks.text: Because exhaust and transfer ports are open together, some fresh mixture flows straight out of the exhaust (short-circuiting). That raw petrol is why the old two-stroke scooter was smoky and thirsty. A deflector on the piston crown (cross scavenging) or ports angled to loop the charge up and round the cylinder (loop scavenging) reduce the loss.

A two-stroke diesel scavenges with air only, so short-circuited air wastes no fuel; fuel is injected after the ports close. It does not use crankcase compression, because the crankcase must hold the lubricating oil. A scavenge blower (often a Roots blower) or a turbocharger supplies air above atmospheric pressure to an air box round the cylinder.

In uniflow scavenging, air enters through ports all round the bottom of the liner and leaves through exhaust valves in the head, so it sweeps the cylinder in one direction. Large marine and power-station engines, the biggest IC engines built, work this way, at around 100 rev/min. Scavenging methods and their efficiencies are taught with supercharging, in the unit on cooling, lubrication and supercharging.

At the same speed a two-stroke cylinder fires twice as often as a four-stroke cylinder: once per revolution against once per two revolutions. In theory it gives twice the power from the same size; in practice part of the stroke is lost to the ports, scavenging is imperfect and some charge escapes, so the real gain is well short of double.

blocks.text: More strokes are also possible. A six-stroke design adds a second expansion (for example steam made by spraying water on the hot cylinder) and a second exhaust; its cycle lasts 6 × 180° = 1080°CA, three revolutions. Such engines are still research and niche machines.

figure.caption: A crankcase-scavenged two-stroke with the piston near BDC. The exhaust port has opened and the burnt gas is leaving; the transfer port has just opened and the charge compressed in the crankcase flows up and sweeps the cylinder. Every revolution has a power stroke, every 20 ms at 3000 rev/min.

examples.question: A four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rev/min. Find the power strokes per second per cylinder and the time for one cycle. Repeat for a two-stroke engine at the same speed.
steps: Four-stroke: one cycle per two revolutions, so 50/2 = 25 cycles per second, that is 25 power strokes per second per cylinder.
Two-stroke: one cycle per revolution, so 50 power strokes per second per cylinder.
examples.answer: Four-stroke: 25 power strokes/s, cycle 40 ms. Two-stroke: 50 power strokes/s, cycle 20 ms.

examples.question: Two single-cylinder engines of 150 cm³ run at 5000 rev/min. The four-stroke has an indicated mep of 6 bar. The two-stroke, because of its ports and short-circuiting, has 4.5 bar. Find the indicated power of each.
steps: Work per cycle = mep × V<sub>s</sub>. Four-stroke: 6 × 10⁵ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ = 90 J. Two-stroke: 4.5 × 10⁵ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ = 67.5 J.
Ratio: 5.63/3.75 = 1.5. With equal mep it would have been 7.5 kW, exactly double.
examples.answer: Four-stroke 3.75 kW; two-stroke 5.63 kW, 1.5 times as much, not twice.

traps: A two-stroke cycle does have exactly two strokes, one up and one down. The point is that each stroke does two jobs: compression above and induction below on the way up, power and gas exchange on the way down.
A two-stroke fires once per revolution and a four-stroke once per two revolutions. “Twice as often” is per second at the same speed, not “twice per revolution”.
Do not double the two-stroke power blindly; port losses and scavenging losses keep the real gain well short of double (1.5 times in the second worked example).
Scavenging is not supercharging. Scavenging sweeps burnt gas out with fresh charge; supercharging raises the density of the charge.
Two-stroke diesels do not use crankcase scavenging; they use a blower, and the big ones use uniflow with exhaust valves.

quiz.q: How many crankshaft revolutions make one cycle of a four-stroke and of a two-stroke engine?
Name the three ports of a crankcase-scavenged two-stroke engine.
quiz.a: Inlet port (into the crankcase), transfer port (crankcase to cylinder) and exhaust port (cylinder to exhaust).

quiz.q: What is a transfer port and when does it open?
quiz.a: The passage from the crankcase to the cylinder. The piston uncovers it near BDC, after the exhaust port has opened, so the compressed crankcase charge flows in and sweeps out the burnt gas.

quiz.q: Why does a two-stroke diesel not use crankcase compression?
quiz.a: Its crankcase holds the lubricating oil, which the scavenge air would carry into the cylinder. A separate blower supplies the scavenge air instead.

quiz.q: A four-stroke four-cylinder engine runs at 1500 rev/min. Find the total number of power strokes per second.
quiz.a: 1500/60 = 25 rev/s. Per cylinder 25/2 = 12.5 per s; four cylinders give 50 power strokes per second.

quiz.q: A single-cylinder two-stroke runs at 6000 rev/min. Find its cycle time and power strokes per second.
quiz.a: 6000/60 = 100 rev/s, so 100 power strokes per second and a cycle time of 1/100 s = 10 ms.

quiz.q: Why does a two-stroke petrol engine emit more unburnt hydrocarbons than a four-stroke?
quiz.a: During scavenging the exhaust and transfer ports are open together, so some fresh mixture flows straight into the exhaust. The loss is worst at light load, when the slow, weak scavenging leaves the charge unevenly mixed and misfires are common.

quiz.q: Compare the cooling needs of four-stroke and two-stroke engines of the same size and speed.
quiz.a: The two-stroke has a power stroke every revolution, so it releases more heat per second into the same cylinder walls and its piston crown never gets an idle stroke to cool. It needs more cooling for the same size.

beyond: Opposed-piston two-strokes, with two pistons in one cylinder and no cylinder head, are being developed for trucks and range extenders because they lose little heat. Direct injection has brought small two-strokes back in some markets by injecting fuel after the exhaust port closes. Search for opposed-piston engine, scavenging efficiency and trapping efficiency.
